Good morning, colleagues. Please take a seat. The fifth meeting of the Third Committee of the General Assembly at its 81st session is called to order. I now invite the committee to continue its general debate. I wish to remind delegations to strictly adhere to the time limits of 10 minutes for interventions by individual delegations. To assist speakers in managing their time, a timer is visible on the screen. The microphones will be automatically switched off when the time is up. I thank you for your cooperation. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sri Lanka.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Good morning. At the outset, allow me to congratulate Ambassador Larsen on his election as the Chair of the Third Committee and to extend my congratulations to the other members of the Bureau. Sri Lanka extends its fullest support and cooperation to you all. Sri Lanka aligns itself with the statement delivered by the distinguished representative of Uruguay on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. Madam Chair, this committee focuses on important aspects and factors impacting people's lives. Its agenda reaches into the lives of children and women, older persons and persons with disabilities, refugees and migrants, and communities living with the consequences of discrimination and exclusion. This December marks 60 years since the adoption of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Together, they remind us of the breadth of the rights we have undertaken to protect. They also remind us that commitments must translate into improving people's everyday lives. Madam Chair, last November in Doha, the international community renewed its commitment to place people at the center of social progress. Sri Lanka welcomed the Doha Political Declaration. The task before us now is to translate those commitments into action. Recent years have demonstrated Sri Lanka, the vulnerability of ordinary families to crisis. Our people carried the burden of a severe economic crisis. Soon after, Cyclone Dikta brought further losses to communities across our island. These experiences have reinforced our belief that social progress must be felt in people's lives. Poverty has many dimensions. It can affect a child's education and a family's health, and as a result, cause an adverse impact on a whole community. That understanding is at the heart of our Praja Shakti national initiative. Nearly 14,000 community development councils have been established across Sri Lanka, giving communities a direct role in identifying local priorities and helping shape the projects intended to improve their lives. People themselves understand the needs of their communities, and a government works best when it listens to them. This year also marks 20 years since the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Sri Lanka has the honour of presiding over the 19th session of its Conference of State Parties. That experience reinforced our conviction that inclusion should be part of how policies and public services are crafted from the beginning. Madam Chair, Sri Lanka has a proud history of women in national leadership. We gave the world its first woman prime minister, and today a woman again holds that office. Our Parliament also has more women members than at any point in our history. The Women's Empowerment Act and the establishment of our National Commission on Women have strengthened our national framework. Madam Chair, we have an enormous responsibility to our children. For most, the first source of care and security is the family, supported by the community around it. Sri Lanka has offered free education for generations. alongside universal healthcare, and we are now reforming our schools so that children are prepared for a rapidly changing world, including changes in the way people work. Our aim is that no child leaves school before completing 13 years of education, and that every child can find the path suited to its academic or vocational abilities. As a State Party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child and its first two Optional Protocols, as well as the key International Labour Organization Conventions concerning child labour, Sri Lanka remains firmly committed to upholding its international obligations and standards relating to the protection and promotion of the rights and well-being of children. Child protection remains a key priority of the government of Sri Lanka, which maintains a policy of zero tolerance towards sexual and gender-based violence. As a member of the Pathfinding Global Alliance to End Violence Against Children, Sri Lanka continues to advance legal, policy, and institutional reforms to strengthen the protection of children from all forms of violence, abuse, and exploitation. We pay particular attention to children who start further behind. The recently launched Diviata Saviak program focuses on young people leaving child development centers. Sri Lanka is working on opening savings accounts for children growing up in child development centres, helping ensure that they enter adulthood with something of their own. The circumstances of a person's childhood should not set the limits of their future. Madam Chair, to live well, people must also feel that they belong. Sri Lanka is a tapestry of different religions, languages, ethnic communities, and cultural traditions. Our history has shown us the cost of division and the importance of rebuilding social cohesion. Our constitution guarantees equality before the law and prohibits discrimination on grounds including race, religion, language, caste, and sex. Sri Lanka remains committed to safeguarding the rights and dignity of every community and to build a society founded on equality, non-discrimination and mutual respect for all. As this year marks 25 years since the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, we reaffirm our commitment to the principles enshrined in the DDPA and to strengthening our collective resolve to build societies where diversity is respected, equality is advanced, and every human being can live with dignity and hope. Madam Chair, as a State Party to all nine core human rights conventions, Sri Lanka has demonstrated a steadfast commitment to protecting and promoting human rights through decades of consistent, transparent and meaningful engagement with the United Nations human rights regular mechanisms. Sri Lanka constructively engaged with the delegation of the UN Sub-Committee on Prevention of Torture during its second visit to Sri Lanka from 15 to 24 June 2026. On 14 August 2026, Sri Lanka engaged in an interactive dialogue during its initial review by the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. In conclusion, the work of this Committee will be judged far from this room, in homes and communities around the world. Sri Lanka reiterates its firm belief that the work of this Committee will be vital to shaping a future that is more just, equitable and inclusive. Therefore, let us recommit to the vision of the Charter and work collectively towards building a United Nations that delivers meaningful results and positively impacts the lives of people around the world. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Sri Lanka. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belarus.

Thank you, Madam Chairperson. The third committee is a platform where we should find common responses to common challenges. Yet over the last few years, we've seen a different picture. The committee's work is being polarized. This is not an isolated phenomenon. It's the direct consequence of global politics going down a negative spiral. The deeper contradictions between states, the more difficult it is for us to come to an agreement here within these walls. Confrontation is replacing cooperation. Politicized resolutions are replacing genuine dialogue. This is particularly obvious in the human rights sphere. Double standards, selective approaches, branding certain countries this, that, or the other. This does not strengthen, but undermines trust in the UN human rights system. We stand convinced this cannot go on. We speak three specific problems in this sphere. First, confrontational country resolutions and mandates, which duplicate one another, hijack the agenda. promote false narratives and have nothing to do with objective reality. They, in fact, facilitate the liquidity crisis getting worse and blocking opportunities for affected states to cooperate with the UN human rights system. A shining example of this is the politicized resolution of the Human Rights Council 61/26 on Belarus, which not only extended the country mandates which duplicate each other, on which millions of US dollars are spent every year, but also pave the way for additional reporting and interactive dialogues. These mandates are based on politicized narratives, not an objective assessment. They are a tool of political pressure, not objective monitoring. Such approaches are being used not just against Belarus, they're also used to exert pressure on many other states, including Venezuela, Iran, DPRK, Myanmar, Nicaragua, Russia, and Eritrea. The second problem is double standards. The joint report by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Belarus and Russia on the human rights situation in Western countries, published in June, clearly shows that those who portray themselves as defenders and, in fact, leaders in the human rights sphere themselves contravene these rights. This document reports serious systemic violations of human rights in specific countries, which, unfortunately, has elicited no response from the Human Rights Council. The third problem is ignoring the priorities of developing countries, ensuring the economic, social, and cultural rights, including the right to development, rooting out racism, xenophobia, protecting families, and countering illegal UCMs. We stand convinced. We need to do away with politicized country resolutions. We need not vilify countries. We need genuine dialogue because there are no countries that are perfect in terms of human rights. That's why Belarus reasserts its openness to dialogue with all human rights mechanisms which respect the sovereign equality of states and the principle of non-interference in internal affairs. The main intergovernmental mechanism for considering human rights issues across all countries without exception has always been and remains the Universal Periodic Review, something Belarus regularly undertakes. Madam Chairperson, the second host of problems is migration and refugees. Here we see those very same double standards and two specific problems, first, distorting the root causes. Wars and conflicts waged by Western countries in developing states are giving rise to new waves of migrants and refugees. Those who started these conflicts should shoulder responsibility for their consequences, instead of laying the blame at the door of others, as some of our neighbors are trying to do. accusing us of instrumentalising migration for political purposes. The second problem is double standards in terms of actions that are taken. On one side, Western countries are calling on everyone to uphold IHL and other international standards as regards refugees and migrants. On the other hand, there are some EU countries which are erecting physical barriers. They are forcing refugees and migrants out of their borders. This is something we're seeing on our own Western border. By contrast, Belarus is providing full access to our border for specialized bodies such as the International Organization for Migration, the UNHCR, the WHO, and the ICRC. Belarusian customs officials, together with medics, are proactively providing assistance to migrants who need such medical assistance. Having said that, the Republic of Belarus is not only open, we are ourselves taking active steps to control migration flows. Over the last five years, we've cracked down on 130 international illegal migration channels. We've detained 300 organizers and facilitators and roughly 1,500 illegal migrants. This work would be even more effective if not the inaction, the absence of answers to our requests and, in some instances, the direct obstruction of some European countries. And this despite the fact that migrants crossing the EU border from Belarus stands at less than half a percent from the overall quantity of illegal migrants entering the EU. That's very telling. We call on states politicizing the suffering and pain of refugees and migrants to revert to upholding international law, civilized professional work, and in good faith cooperation. Madam Chairperson, the third topic, which touches upon many issues falling within the purview of the third committee, is misuse of technologies. New challenges thrown up by digitalization are disquieting, in particular, human smuggling so as to force these people to partake in crimes. The mechanism is very easy. Technologies are used to enlist victims, to force them to commit crimes. This type of human trafficking is on the rise exponentially. So it's already taken over Asia and is now shifting to Latin America and other continents. Belarus and Kazakhstan. working at the 35th session of the UN Commission on Crime Prevention in Vienna in June of this year, Kazakhstan and Belarus put forward a joint resolution. The problem was and remains very pertinent to the International Day for Combating Human Trafficking. And it was also front and center of the work of the Working Group on Countering Human Trafficking, which took place in June in Vienna. We need to implement the provisions of the resolution and the recommendations of the Working Group, so as to ensure we effectively counter this new threat. Belarus will continue placing priority attention to the issue of human trafficking, including through coordinating the work of the Group of Friends, which are combating human trafficking. Madam Chairperson, last but not least, some are politicizing human rights. Meanwhile, Belarus is genuinely defending them through social policies. We're supporting older persons, persons with disabilities, veterans, large families, and other vulnerable groups who are an important segment of the Belarusian development model. We are particularly attentive to providing tailored assistance to those who find themselves in a difficult situation. For us, strong families is the pillar of our society and demographic safety. That's why our policy, in deed and not just in word, creates the conditions for having and rearing children, supporting parents, and protecting mothers. 2026 has been proclaimed the Year of the Belarusian Woman in Belarus. When we discuss the status of women, families and children, we need to factor in the cultural and spiritual traditions of specific States and respect their right to independently set their social policies. That's why we've taken this as the foundation for our work in the Third Committee. We've said that the work of the Third Committee is being politicized, but this is not a life sentence. Belarus stands ready to work constructively with all delegations on the basis of equal rights, mutual respect and no double standards. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Belarus. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bangladesh.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on your election and assure you of Bangladesh's full support and cooperation. Bangladesh aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. Madam Chair, we meet at a time when the very principles on which this committee work are under severe strain. We are witnessing a frontal attack on established rules of international law alongside an acute funding shortfall. Fundamental human rights and humanitarian norms are being violated with impunity or applied selectively. The human cost is high. Public trust in the United Nations and confidence in international law is at an all-time low. But all is not lost yet. We have been encouraged by the many voices in this session's general debate that have stood firmly for multilateralism, respect for international law, and the principles of the UN Charter. We share their commitments. Drawing strength from the general debate, we call for a stronger focus on the implementation of commitments and an honest assessment of the results. Our work should be measured by one question: does it improve the lives and protect the rights of people? Madam Chair, civil, political, economic and social rights are universal, indivisible and interdependent. That is not a trite statement, but a tried and tested formula for effective social development. Bangladesh has significantly increased its investment in women and girls' education, health and livelihood skills, and youth development as concrete means of empowering women and young people to exercise their rights fully and participate equally in economic, social, and public life. We acknowledge that sexual and gender-based violence, discrimination, and unequal access to economic opportunities remain key barriers to gender equality in Bangladesh and globally. More efforts must be made to implement the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, the obligations under CEDAW and the commitments of SDG 5. The rights, safety and dignity of women migrant workers must be protected throughout the migration cycle. More must also be done to advance women's meaningful participation in conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and peace processes. Madam Chair, Bangladesh was born from a struggle for equality, dignity, and social justice. These principles are integral to our national life and constitutional values. We reaffirm the rights of people to self-determination and support the Palestinian people's right to self-determination and an independent, viable, and sovereign state of Palestine. As we mark the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development, Bangladesh reaffirms its support towards the legally binding International Covenant on the Right to Development. Bangladesh is a party to the nine core international human rights instruments, We remain committed to fulfilling our obligations under these instruments and strengthening our national institutions and legal framework. Bangladesh has recently enacted legislation to improve its national human rights institution and strengthen protection against enforced disappearances. We believe strong national institutions, the rule of law, and accountability are essential for the protection of human rights. and must be carried out in consultation with citizens, civil society, and other key stakeholders. Madam Chair, racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance remain serious challenges. We oppose all forms of racial discrimination and must ensure equality and dignity for all. The 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action provides an opportunity to renew this commitment, Bangladesh supports its full and effective implementation. Madam Chair, rapid advances in artificial intelligence and other technologies are changing our societies, creating both opportunities and risks. AI can enhance research and access to education, healthcare, and other services. But without equitable access and responsible governance, it can also deepen existing inequalities and create new risks. The Third Committee should contribute to the debate on these issues across the full spectrum of human rights, social development, and humanitarian concerns. Technological progress must remain human-centered and must not come at the expense of human dignity, equality, and fundamental freedoms. Madam Chair, Bangladesh is deeply concerned about the underfunding of human rights, humanitarian, and development programs. Diverting funds from development to defense weakens both security and human rights, as the root causes of conflict are often to be found in economic, social, and political grievances. Peace and security, sustainable development, and human rights are mutually reinforcing pillars of the United Nations. Can a house stand when two out of three pillars are weakened? While conflicts are proliferating, humanitarian needs are rising, but humanitarian assistance is shrinking. Madam Chair, we must insist on full respect for the protection of civilians, for adequate humanitarian assistance, and for safe, timely, and unhindered humanitarian access. As new crises emerge, the world must not forget the plight of those who languish in refugee camps for years, such as the Rohingya in Bangladesh. The social, economic, and environmental costs have been high. But the human costs for the displaced and their host communities are even higher. We call for sustained international support for the Rohingya and a predictable action plan towards their safe, voluntary, and dignified return to Myanmar. Finally, Madam Chair, allow me to reiterate that this committee must not simply adopt resolutions or reaffirm commitments. It is our shared responsibility to ensure that commitments are implemented. We must close the gap between rhetoric and reality, between promise and delivery. Thank you, Madam Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Bangladesh. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Poland.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Poland aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. This year we mark the 60th anniversary of the adoption of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Twenty years ago, the General Assembly established the Human Rights Council and other milestone human rights conventions. These anniversaries remind us that the human rights architecture we rely on today was built by States that chose cooperation over confrontation, and universal standards over the convenience of exceptions. Today, that architecture is under strain, including from deliberate attempts to weaken the very mechanisms designed to hold violators to account. Poland considers human rights to be inherent, universal, indivisible, inviolable, and inalienable. Poland's own history taught us that the lasting peace and security cannot be built without democracy, the rule of law, and good governance. That is why Poland consistently promotes democratic values and the principles of good governance as a foundation of sustainable peace and security in the United Nations and beyond. This is also why, at the Human Rights Council, Poland, together with its core group partners, continues to lead the work on good governance, this year with a focus on the use of new technologies, including artificial intelligence, in public administration. Madam Chair. Poland remains a firm supporter of a strong, independent and effective UN human rights system. We stand by the independence of the Human Rights Council, its special procedures and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. We remain committed to strengthening the treaty body system. Our engagement is long-term. Poland, for the fourth time now, has presented its candidature to the Human Rights Council for the term 2029-2031. We seek membership in order to contribute actively to shaping international standards and the Council's response to human rights situations, in a spirit of dialogue, but without compromising on principles. Madam Chair, the human rights situation in Ukraine, the Russian Federation and Belarus remains a particular focus for Poland. More than four and a half years into Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine, civilians continue to bear the gravest consequences. We will continue to draw the attention of the international community to the crimes and violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law committed by the Russian armed forces and armed groups under their control. These include torture, sexual violence, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance in the temporarily occupied territories, as well as the ill-treatment of prisoners of war. Ukrainian children forcibly transferred or deported to Russia must be returned to their families without delay. Any just and lasting peace must be grounded in international law, the UN Charter and accountability. The violations committed abroad are inseparable from repression at home. In the Russian Federation, dissent is criminalised, while human rights defenders and independent journalists are imprisoned or forced into exile. In Belarus, the authorities continue to persecute political opponents, civil society and independent media, as well as members of national minorities. We call on Belarus to release all political prisoners and to cease the instrumentalisation of migrants. The UN mechanisms monitoring these situations, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, the Special Rapporteurs on the Russian Federation and on Belarus, and the Group of Independent Experts on Belarus, play a replaceable role in documenting violations and preserving evidence for future justice. Ensuring their adequate and stable funding is a priority. Poland pays particular attention to those most exposed to exclusion and violence, including children and persons with disabilities. Poland was proud to lead the work on Security Council Resolution 2475, dedicated to the protection of persons with disabilities in armed conflict. On the 20th anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, we call for its full implementation, including in humanitarian action and post-conflict recovery. Madam Chair, Poland remains committed to promoting freedom of religion or belief and to countering all related forms of intolerance, hatred and discrimination, including against religious minorities. It was in this spirit that we initiated the General Assembly resolution, adopted by consensus, establishing the International Day commemorating the victims of acts of violence based on religion or belief. We are increasingly concerned about the negative impact of disinformation on the enjoyment of human rights. Information manipulation fuels hatred, undermines trust in democratic institutions, and is used as a tool of hostile interference. Countering it effectively must go hand in hand with full respect for freedom of expression. Poland remains deeply concerned about the humanitarian situation in Gaza, as well as about the violence in the West Bank. We call for the protection of civilians at all times and for safe and unhindered humanitarian access. We are equally alarmed by the atrocities against civilians in Sudan, including widespread conflict-related sexual violence, and by the continued persecution of the Rohingya and other minorities in Myanmar. Madam Chair, Poland supports the UN80 initiative and efforts to make our organization more efficient and effective. Reform, however, must strengthen, not weaken, the ability of the United Nations to deliver on its mandates. The human rights pillar, which receives less than 1% of the UN regular budget, has already been disproportionately affected by this year's cuts. The continuity, independence, transparency, effectiveness, and stable and sustainable funding for the human rights pillar must be preserved. And yet a strong, sustainably funded human rights system is a condition of the credibility of the entire United Nations. Madam Chair, 60 years ago, states from all regions recognized in the covenants that the ideal of free human beings enjoying freedom from fear and want can only be achieved if everyone can enjoy all their rights. Our task in this committee is not to renegotiate that promise, but to keep it. Poland stands ready to work constructively with all delegations to this end. With this, I have the honor of passing the floor to Poland's youth delegates who will deliver the remainder of the statement.

Madam Chair, Excellencies, I have the honor to speak to you on behalf of Poland as a youth delegate. More than 80 years ago, in the aftermath of two world wars, member states built something extraordinary. A system in which international law, rather than force, would govern relations between states. Today, that foundation is under strain. Wars continue to destroy lives and communities. At the end of 2025, almost 118 million people were forcibly displaced worldwide. The reality of global crisis remind us of one uncomfortable truth. Having rights today does not guarantee that we will have them tomorrow. As privileged as I feel standing before you today, I cannot stop thinking about young people around the world who have more ambition, talent, and dreams, yet far fewer opportunities simply because of where they were born. They may be a girl in Afghanistan, denied access to education and public life, a child in South Sudan, forced into a conflict they never chose, or a young Ukrainian refugee in Poland, trying to rebuild her life. The circumstances are different, but the principle is the same. Human rights cannot depend on geography. Excellencies, Polish youth call for a future where every young person can realize their potential, no matter where they are born. And we call on this committee to remember the lesson that gave rise to the UN Charter. When power prevails over rules, human lives pay the price. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland. Sorry.

Mr. Distinguished delegates, in the 20th century we witnessed the tragedy of the two world wars and the emergence of terrifying new technologies. The international community responded with a clear promise, never again. Yet today, that promise has been once again broken by the Russian Federation. Since 2022, Russia has systematically deported thousands of Ukrainian children from occupied territories, placing them in Russian homes, stripping them of their names, language, and identity. The risk of Russian aggression is, however, but one existential risk facing our generation. We are on the cusp of artificial intelligence improving itself autonomously with years worth of progress squeezed into weeks. We have already seen AI agents carry out cyber attacks. Humankind is at risk of losing control over this technology and the ongoing arms race. At the same time, artificial intelligence holds enormous potential to accelerate scientific discovery, a foundation built by Polish scientists who led the development of the pioneering transformer architecture and ChatGPT. Because no single national or regional framework can govern such a revolutionary technology which will define our generation's future. This is precisely where multilateralism must prove its value. Therefore, as a youth delegate, I call for stronger international cooperation to ensure that AI is developed and used safely, respects human rights, and benefits young people. Second, intensified efforts to locate Ukrainian children, deported or forcibly transferred by Russia, secure their return, and reunite them with their families. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ireland.

Thank you, Chair. Ireland aligns with the EU statement. The multilateral system, anchored in the United Nations Charter, is at the core of Ireland's foreign policy. Fundamental to that multilateral order is the international human rights system, based on the concept of indivisible and universal human rights. Together, the UN Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights have laid the foundation for an international order which, however imperfect and challenged, provide the basis for individuals to live their lives freely and without discrimination, for peaceful settlement of disputes and non-aggression, and for a fairer, more equal world. Millions of lives have improved through the promotion of all human rights, including civil and political and economic, social and cultural rights. In the 40 years since the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development, we have made remarkable progress. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 2.6 billion to 826 million. To achieve further progress, including in development, we must remain committed to progressing all human rights. That is why, in the context of UN80, our work must be not just more efficient, but also more effective and human-centred. To achieve this, the UN's human rights pillar must be protected and strengthened, including by providing OHCHR with the necessary political and financial support. Ireland was pleased to play its part this year, working with Senegal as co-facilitators on the review, which resulted in consensus reaffirmation of the status of the Human Rights Council, welcomed ongoing coordination between the General Assembly and the Human Rights Council, and recalled the importance of its adequate and sustainable financing. Chair, I will focus on five areas which are priorities for Ireland in our work at the United Nations, including in seeking election to the Human Rights Council. First, the protection of civil society and human rights defenders, including their safe and meaningful participation in the work of the UN, where they bring expertise, transparency, accountability and lived experience to our work. As Member States, we share a responsibility to protect and promote civil society's participation as an essential element of our work on human rights and prevent and address reprisals. Today's context of ever more frequent violations of international law requires accountability. Recent sanctions and the diplomatic campaign against the International Criminal Court represent an unacceptable interference with the sovereign decision of States parties to put an end to impunity for the most serious international crimes and an unprecedented attack on independent legal officers simply for carrying out professional responsibilities that we have entrusted to them. We call for all measures that harm the Court and those that work for it to be withdrawn and for all States to respect the Court's independence and integrity. Second, Ireland will continue to champion women's rights and gender equality. Protection of the rights of all women and girls is fundamental for sustainable social and economic growth and development. Gender equality remains a core tenet of Ireland's work on human rights, peacebuilding, development and cooperation. Ireland is also fully committed to sexual and reproductive rights, including maternal health, and to reaching the furthest behind first. Nowhere are the rights of women and girls more abjectly denied than in Afghanistan, where women and girls are systematically excluded from society, denied basic rights to education, employment, freedom of movement and access to services. The Taliban's horrific oppression of women and girls is an affront to basic freedoms and human dignity. Third, the right of LGBTIQ+ persons globally. From our experience in recent decades, we know that society is richer when the human rights of all are respected. We will advocate for decriminalisation of same-sex relations and repeal of discriminatory legal provisions. as we did domestically in Ireland. We will also continue to support the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons to development cooperation funding. Fourth, the fundamental right to adequate food. The fight for food security is being lost, with humanitarian crises fuelled by conflict, climate change, and geopolitical and economic dynamics. We see the right to food and the fundamental right to be free from hunger being denied around the world. In Gaza and in Sudan, famine is being created and inflected on fellow humans. In Yemen, hunger has been used as a weapon of war. In the Black Sea, grain exports have been intentionally imperiled by Russia, with devastating consequences for global food supplies. We also see the effects climate change is wreaking on food security. Fifth, the right of persons with disabilities in conflict. A human rights-based approach across the fields of humanitarian assistance, disarmament, conflict resolution, and peacebuilding is needed to address the disproportionate impact of conflict on persons with disabilities. Ireland continues to highlight this issue, including by advocating for implementation of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and effective implementation of the OEWPA declaration. Chair, 25 years after the Durban Declaration, the scourge of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance remains a lived reality for far too many. Ireland condemns all forms and manifestations of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, including anti-Semitism, anti-Muslim hatred and hatred of Christians, Ireland will work with all partners to build societies founded on equality, non-discrimination, respect, inclusion and human dignity for all. We must also seek action on and accountability for egregious denials of human rights in the world today. Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine has been accompanied by widespread, well-documented human rights violations. These include arbitrary detention, torture and sexual violence against civilians, including children, indoctrination, sham elections, as well as the forcible transfer and deportation of children. Russia continues its indiscriminate attacks, killing civilians daily, while systematically targeting Ukraine's critical infrastructure. Ireland calls on the authorities in Iran to halt all violence against the Iranian people, suspend executions and release those detained during and following the January protests. Ireland is firmly opposed to the death penalty in all circumstances as an affront to human dignity and condemns Iran's extensive use of capital punishment. Ireland joins partners in condemning attempts by Iranian security forces and associated actors to intimidate, threaten or attack individuals abroad, including Iranian dissidents, journalists and Jewish and Israeli communities. I remain concerned by the repression of civil society in China, including the treatment of human rights defenders. These include restrictions on freedom of association and freedom of religion or belief in Xinjiang and Tibet following the introduction of the new law on promoting ethnic unity and progress, and restrictions on freedom of expression in Hong Kong, including the repressive use of the national security law. Ireland condemns the grave abuses and violations of international human rights law in Sudan, particularly the systematic perpetration of conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence against women and girls. We strongly support international accountability efforts towards justice for victims and accountability for perpetrators. The culture of impunity in Sudan must end. The human rights situation in Palestine is unconscionable. In the West Bank, settler violence has reached unprecedented levels, often with the acquiescence of Israeli forces. The E1 settlement poses a fundamental threat to the prospect of a viable and contiguous Palestinian state. Ireland reiterates our call on Israel to immediately cease all settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories, including the recently published E1 tender. Chair, during this session, Ireland holds the presidency of the Council of the European Union. One of our core priorities are our values, including protection and promotion of human rights as the bedrock of our societies. and the foundation of fulfilling, dignified lives. Our presidency motto is the Irish phrase, "Nein ardh, ne cur le cheile", which translates as "There is no strength without unity". We look forward to working with you and all delegations in that spirit. It may not always be easy, but we will play our part to find common cause, to resist backsliding and to make positive progress in the interests of the people we serve, in particular those left furthest behind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ireland. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belgium.

Madam Chairperson, Belgium aligns itself with the EU statement. We would now like to make the following remarks in a national capacity. As we look at the world, we see a disquieting trend. Human dignity and human rights are being viewed as optional or at least secondary to the sovereignty of states. Belgium is participating in this third committee session with a deep conviction. This state of affairs is unacceptable. Ever since they were created, human rights have been a key pillar of the multilateral system, with at its heart the United Nations and its charter. This system is confronting crises requiring our immediate and undivided attention. First, the alarming and unprecedented restriction of civic space. all over the world. This is of concern to us. Independent organizations, civil society, journalists and human rights defenders are the lifeblood of any resilient democracy. Third, the proliferation of conflicts, armed conflicts that are escalating is a factor that is devastating international law, in particular the UN Charter and international humanitarian law as well as international human rights law. We are witnessing attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure. Obstacles to humanitarian access. We're seeing deaths of humanitarian workers. Madam Chairperson, in order to stop this dangerous trajectory in its tracks, Belgium underscores its unwavering commitment to the UN human rights architecture. This year, we marked the 60th anniversary of the International Covenant on Human Rights. And we continue to promote the ratification thereof and the implementation of these rights. Thank you, Chair. Malta aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. Chair, at the outset, allow me to join others in congratulating you and the rest of the Bureau on your election and to thank you for guiding the work of the Third Committee. Denmark aligns itself with the statement made by the European Union. In a world where human rights continue to be violated and fundamental freedoms are under threat, their protection remains a cornerstone of Denmark's foreign policy and international engagement. We continue to be seriously concerned with human rights violations in many corners of the world. Unfortunately, the list of places where human rights are being suppressed is still too long. Persistent wars, conflicts and instability around the world are stark reminders that we must listen to those whose human rights are being violated. Their voices must be heard, and their rights and dignity must remain at the centre of our collective response. Denmark therefore commits to the inclusion of civil society to ensuring genuine opportunities for influence and action. We urge the UN to continue promoting the aims and principles of the Secretary-General's call for action for human rights through an era of reform and the transition to a new Secretary-General. Chair, in closing, we stress the importance of a human rights-based approach to sustainable development as well as to peace and security. Denmark believes that the full realization of human rights is essential to achieving the universal goals of the UN And we must all take action to uphold these goals. Thank you.

On humanitarian action, we remain loyal to our tradition of hosting various refugees and asylum seekers. We are working hand in hand with the High Commissioner for Refugees and humanitarian partners to ensure we afford protection and assistance to these people. Protecting the most vulnerable can only be achieved if we doggedly fight against all forms of discrimination, exclusion and intolerance. We remain unstintingly committed to protecting human dignity, equality and non-discrimination. 25 years after the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, we reiterate our commitment to the implementation of these documents. That is why we are strengthening our legal institutional framework for promoting and protecting rights. Our history, from the struggle for national liberation and independence in 1975, through a prolonged armed conflict to the achievement of peace in 2002, has shaped our understanding that the dignity and well-being of people must remain at the center of the public policy. Since the end of the conflict, Angola has progressively strengthened national institutions and expanded social services with particular attention to health, education, social protection, and inclusion of vulnerable groups. At independence, Angola had only 19 doctors, an acute shortage of nurses, technicians, and adequate health infrastructure. The national health network comprises approximately 320 facilities. Today, the national health service consists of 3,355 health units and 44,222 hospital beds, including 1,609 intensive care beds. While important challenges remain, Angola is committed to strengthening primary health care, improving maternal and child health, expanding access to essential services, and ensuring that technological and medical advances contribute to more equitable health care. We encourage continued international cooperation, including capacity building, technology transfer, and sustainable financing, to assist developing countries in strengthening resilient and inclusive health systems. Education is equally fundamental to the realization of human rights and the achievement of sustainable development. For the 2026-2027 academic year, more than 9.6 million students are enrolled in Angola, supported by more than 126,000 classrooms and 280,000 teachers. As a country with a predominantly young population, Angola attached particular importance to reducing inequalities in access to education and facilitating the transition from education to decent employment. We are therefore expanding technical and vocational education, professional training, internship, entrepreneurship programs, and access to microcredit. Through the National Employment Fund and the Youth and Opportunities for Good Jobs in Angola program, JobAngola, thousands of Young citizens have already benefited from vocational training, employment initiatives, and professional support. Higher education has also expanded, with 106 institutions operating across 19 of Angola's 21 provinces. Scholarship programs continue to provide opportunities to students, including those from economically vulnerable backgrounds. Angola calls for stronger international partnership to address youth employment, the digital divide, and skills gap, particularly in developing countries. Madam Chair, social inclusion remains a central pillar of Angola's national development strategy. We acknowledge the important contribution of the United Nations, including the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, to family reunification and the return and reintegration of Angolan refugees. I thank you.

Hungary condemns grave violations against children in situations of armed conflict, advocating for stronger prevention, protection and accountability, as well as digital safety and integrated child protection systems in the context of violence and sexual exploitation of children. We are committed to promoting the rights of persons with disabilities in all spheres of life, with particular attention to their social inclusion and their inclusive participation in education and the labour market. Hungary is dedicated to the promotion and protection of freedom of religion or belief and combating religious intolerance, incitement of hatred and violence against persons belonging to religious communities, including Christians, and remains firmly committed to combating antisemitism. Madam Chair, the erosion of human rights, the incremental decline in democratic principles, civic spaces, and the rule of law, arbitrary restrictions on freedom of expression and association, persecution of minorities, curtailing the independence of the judiciary are all ominous indicators of impending instability. Human rights and peace are inseparable concepts. Oftentimes, human rights are only an afterthought, a moral aspiration to be addressed only after security and stability are achieved after turbulent times. But incorporating them in every stage of conflict prevention and conflict resolution is essential and must be non-negotiable. In today's global environment, the international community is facing a growing number of crises, including threats to global security, geopolitical tensions, climate change, and humanitarian emergencies. Armed conflicts remains among the most pressing challenges to international peace and security, with Russia's war against Ukraine and the situation in the Middle East continuing to have far-reaching regional and global implications. Hungary emphasizes the importance of comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the principles of international law and supports all efforts aimed at initiatives towards that end. Hungary draws attention to the serious danger the people in Ukraine, including the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia, are living in due to the conflict. We wish to express our solidarity with all those affected by the war and to reiterate Hungary's commitment to the promotion and protection of human rights for all as an indispensable foundation for sustainable peace. Hungary attaches particular importance to the broader stability of the Middle East and supports efforts to prevent further regional escalation and to improve the humanitarian situation. Hungary reaffirms its support to efforts aiming at achieving sustainable peace in the Middle East. Hungary is a committed supporter of constructive dialogue, which is indispensable for achieving peace. The protection of civilians, the improvement of the humanitarian situation in Gaza, and the recognition of the right of self-defense of Israel are prerequisites for the resolution of the conflict. Madam Chair, in conclusion, allow me to reaffirm Hungary's firm commitment to upholding human rights and fundamental freedoms and maintaining inclusive dialogues. We strongly believe that young people must be able to express their ideas, concerns, and priorities. Their participation is crucial to make our world a better place for all. Therefore, for our remaining time, I would like to give the floor to our youth delegate to share his insights.

Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Over the past two years, I spoke with more than 2,000 young Hungarians in the capital and in small towns across the country. What I heard most often was not anger, and it was not ambition. It was indifference. We grew up in a world that changed faster than ever before. Digital addiction, artificial intelligence, social isolation, a deepening mental health crisis. Every morning, the headlines bring war, climate disaster, and political conflict. It is hard to stay motivated in that environment. It is harder to believe that anything you do will matter. So many of them stopped taking part at all, not because they do not care, but because they were convinced their action would change nothing. That belief is the quietest threat to democratic society. A generation that feels powerless cannot be mobilized for peace, for climate action, or for the SDGs. This year, in my country, that began to shift. Participation has more than one door-- local action, entrepreneurship, research, speaking up in public, and the ballot box. This spring, young Hungarians went through that last door in numbers that could not be overlooked. new initiatives followed, and young people started looking for places where they could listen and speak up. And institutions answered. Over the summer, the newly established Ministry of Education and Children began creating a children and youth participation group after consulting more than 30 organizations and experts. The Student Voice Theme Day gives students a structured way to say what they think about the education system that shapes them. These are real steps. They are not yet a culture. Participation is still treated as an invitation, something that can be extended or withdrawn. It should be the baseline. So I ask three things of this committee: build permanent structures, not one of consultations; resource them locally so that minorities and young people far from the capital can reach them and participation does not become another privilege; and measure whether they change decisions, because a seat at the table that changes nothing teaches the same lesson as no seat at all. We want to understand the world before we inherit it, to learn from the problems of today and prepare for those of tomorrow. We would rather do that as partners than alone. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Hungary. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Chair, I join other delegations in congratulating you and members of your Bureau upon your election to the 81st session of the General Assembly. You can count on Malaysia's full support and cooperation throughout the work of this committee. Malaysia aligns itself with the statements of the G77 and China, the OIC, the Group of Friends of the Family, and subsequent statements on specific agenda items by ASEAN. Madam Chair, We meet at a time when the promise of peace, development and human dignity is under mounting strain. Conflicts continue to inflict immense human suffering. Inequalities persist within and among countries. Climate change, demographic shifts and rapid technological transformation are reshaping our societies. At the same time, intolerance and discrimination continue to undermine social cohesion. These challenges remind us that social development and human rights cannot be pursued in isolation from peace and sustainable development, nor can they be advanced through fragmented responses. Malaysia therefore remains committed to a multilateral system anchored in the United Nations Charter, international law, dialogue and cooperation. Madam Chair, at the national level, Malaysia continues to translate the aspirations of the Madani Economy Framework into action through the 13th Malaysia Plan 2026-2030. The plan seeks to strengthen Malaysia's economic potential and competitiveness while ensuring that the benefits of growth are shared more broadly. It places particular emphasis on improving living standards, enhancing social mobility, and ensuring a decent quality of life for all. This efforts are underpinned by good governance, integrity and accountability. Together, they reflect our commitment to inclusive and sustainable development that delivers tangible improvements in the lives of our people. This commitment is being translated into action through the National Social Policy Action Plan 2026-2030, launched earlier this year. The plan brings together all ministries and agencies in implementing 102 initiatives centred on four prevention, empowerment, promotion, and protection. Together, these initiatives aim to strengthen social well-being and respond more effectively to the needs of vulnerable groups. Malaysia is also preparing for important demographic transitions. The National Action Plan for Older Persons 2026-2030 guides our efforts to strengthen long-term care and community-based support. At the same time, the National Action Plan on Children 2026-2030 to strengthen child protection and promote safe and inclusive environments, including in the digital sphere. These efforts reflect our conviction that development must respond to the needs of people throughout the life course. Madam Chair, Malaysia remains steadfast in advancing the empowerment of women and girls. The National Women's Policy and Women's Development Action Plan 2025-2030 continue to guide our efforts to enhance women's participation and leadership, strengthen economic opportunities, and address discrimination and violence against women and girls. Malaysia has also taken an important step towards greater equality in citizenship rights through amendments to our federal constitution. The reform provides for children born overseas to Malaysian mothers and non-citizen fathers to acquire citizenship by operation of law upon the relevant provisions coming into operation. Necessary legal and administrative preparations are being undertaken to give effect to the amended constitutional provisions. The reform reflects reflects Malaysia's continuing efforts to strengthen the protection and well-being of women, children and families. Madam Chair, Malaysia's diversity remains one of our greatest strength. As a multi-ethnic, multicultural, and multi-religious society, we know from experience that unity cannot be taken for granted. It must continually be nurtured through mutual respect, understanding, and dialogue. In this regard, Malaysia has introduced the National Unity Ministry Strategic Plan which places renewed emphasis on nation building, social integration, and strengthening national values. This commitment assumes even greater importance amid the persistence of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance worldwide. As we mark the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action only days ago, Malaysia underscored that all forms of prejudice persist, even as new manifestations emerge, including through digital hate speech, religious profiling and Islamophobia. The international community must reject hatred and intolerance in all their forms and renew our collective commitment to equality Madam Chair, Malaysia remains deeply appalled by the atrocities committed across the occupied Palestinian territory. In Gaza, civilians continue to be killed and humanitarian needs remain immense. restrictions on humanitarian access continue to impede the delivery of life-saving assistance. In the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, settlement expansion, settler violence, displacement, and movement restrictions continue to undermine the prospects for peace. The international community has the responsibility to ensure the full and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance, the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel. Malaysia reaffirms the indispensable role of UNRWA and rejects any attempt to undermine its mandate or operations. International law and international humanitarian law must be upheld. Accountability for Israel's unlawful action against the Palestinian people must remain a priority. It is fundamental to justice, to preventing the recurrence of violations, and to achieving a just and lasting peace. Malaysia reiterates its unwavering support for the Palestinian people in the exercise of their inalienable rights, including their right to self-determination. the United Nations. Malaysia remains steadfast in its support for the establishment of an independent and sovereign state of Palestine based on the pre-1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital. A just and lasting peace can only be achieved through a comprehensive solution that upholds the rights, dignity, and legitimate aspirations of the Palestinian people. In conclusion, Malaysia will continue to engage constructively in this committee and across the United Nations system, guided by the principles of the UN Charter, we remain committed to advancing social progress, protecting human dignity, and strengthening international cooperation so that our collective efforts deliver meaningful improvements in the lives of all people. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Latvia.

Thank you. Madam Chair, let me begin by extending our sincere congratulations to you and the Bureau members on your election. You can count on Latvia's full support throughout this session. Latvia aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union and would like to add following remarks in our national capacity. Latvia approaches the work of the CERT Committee with the understanding that all three pillars of the United Nations are equally important and mutually reinforcing. Human rights are not a separate agenda, but a necessity for peace, security, and sustainable development. Likewise, it is our firm conviction that human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated. The proliferation of armed conflict, effects of climate change, emerging threats, and pushback against gender equality creates a world where hard-won progress on the rights of women and girls is slowly eroding. The situations in Afghanistan, Myanmar, Haiti, Sudan, Yemen, and elsewhere show that women's rights are never secondary or conditional. They are completely inseparable from global peace and stability. Taking into account these circumstances, Latvia will continue to advocate for the elimination of all forms of gender inequality, including through addressing discriminatory laws, combating gender stereotypes, and overcoming harmful social norms. Latvia will place particular emphasis on advancing efforts aimed at preventing and eliminating sexual and gender-based violence, including conflict-related sexual violence. Latvia will actively support initiatives that promote the effective implementation of UN Security Council resolutions on women, peace and security. Despite decades of evidence, women's participation in peace processes remains an exception rather than the norm. Latvia will continue to advocate for the full integration of the gender perspective across the work of the UN, as well as the full, equal and meaningful participation of women in peace and security efforts. Furthermore, Latvia will advocate for the economic empowerment of women and girls through quality, accessible, equal, affordable, and gender-responsive education. Starting from early childhood, such education should challenge gender stereotypes, discriminatory social norms, foster women's leadership skills and girls' and women's STEM competencies. Madam Chair, during this third committee session, accountability will remain one of the Latvia's key priorities. Latvia remains committed to ending impunity and ensuring accountability for all violations of international law, including international human rights law, international criminal law, and international humanitarian law. Latvia condemns in the strongest possible terms the atrocities committed in Ukraine by Russia. Russia's illegal war of aggression constitutes a serious breach of international law, including core provisions of the UN Charter. Latvia condemns in the strongest possible terms Russia's continued deliberate targeting of Ukrainian civilians and civilian infrastructure, including electricity and water facilities, as well as humanitarian and medical facilities. Such actions violate international humanitarian law and may constitute war crimes. Latvia also condemns in the strongest possible terms arbitrary detention, extrajudicial executions, enforced disappearances, widespread and systematic torture of civilian detainees and prisoners of war, sexual violence, unlawful deportation and forcible transfers of Ukrainian civilians, including children, as well as restrictions on religious freedom, culture, education, identity and cultural heritage imposed by Russia in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. Madam Chair, Latvia will continue to support relevant resolutions and initiatives aimed at ensuring accountability for violations committed in the context of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, and at maintaining international attention on the human rights situation in Ukraine stemming from Russia's war of aggression. More broadly, Latvia will actively support initiatives aimed at strengthening accountability for violations of international law and calls on all states to cooperate fully with UN human rights mechanisms, with a view to ensuring accountability and delivering justice for victims and survivors. Latvia is concerned by the use of hybrid tactics and threats to undermine democracies and obstruct the enjoyment of human rights. We see the increasing impact on human rights of the deliberate creation and dissemination of false and manipulated information intended to deceive and mislead audiences, either to cause harm or for political gain. Namely, Latvia opposes the use of the pretext of fighting Nazism by Russia, including through its annual resolution to both distort history, and conceal the real goal behind its unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression against Ukraine, aiming to justify it. These actions undermine the genuine fight against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and all forms of racial intolerance, including Nazism and neo-Nazism. Latvia also condemns the deliberate exploitation of vulnerable people by Belarus to exert political and physical pressure on its neighboring states and the European Union. For more than five years, Latvia has been exposed to deliberate instrumentalization of migrants by Belarus in complicity with Russia to undermine our territorial integrity and national security. These actions openly disregard the international human rights order and facilitate that these people become victims of exploitation, trafficking and smuggling. We will continue to call on Belarus to end these practices and respect its obligations under international law. Madam Chair, we also see continued backlash and reprisals against civil society around the world. including repressions, intimidation, threats and arrests. Throughout this session, Latvia will continue to advocate for a safe and enabling environment for civil society and for the meaningful participation of human rights defenders in the work of the UN. Latvia will continue to condemn any form of intimidation and reprisals against those cooperating with the UN system. Latvia stresses the importance of ensuring that human rights defenders are able to promote and protect human rights without fear of reprisals or intimidation of any kind anywhere in the world. Latvia will also support efforts to enhance the full, effective and meaningful participation of Indigenous Peoples' representatives in relevant United Nations meetings and processes concerning issues affecting them. Madam Chair, delegates, in conclusion, allow me to emphasize that Latvia looks forward to working together with delegations during this session to advance these and all aims that are aimed at protecting human rights for all. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Latvia. I now give the floor to the permanent representative of the Republic of Korea.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Let me begin by congratulating you on your election as a chair of the Third Committee. I assure you and the members of the Bureau of my delegation full support. Madam Chair, protected conflicts in Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Myanmar, and beyond continue to take their heaviest toll on the most vulnerable, especially children. According to the Secretary-General's latest report on children and armed conflict, violations against children reached an unprecedented level in 2025, with more than 38,000 verified grave violations against over 24,000 children. Behind each of these figures is a child whose life has been forever changed. In the face of such suffering, the Republic of Korea remains resolute in its commitment to the principles at the heart of this organization: freedom, human rights, inclusiveness, and solidarity. As a member of the Human Rights Council, and drawing on our recent tenure on the Security Council, we will continue to play a leading role in defending and advancing these shared values. Today, My delegation wishes to focus on four priorities: the rights of women and children, and the empowerment of persons with disabilities, human rights in the age of new technologies, and pressing country situations. Protecting and promoting the rights of women and girls, particularly in conflict and crisis settings, remains a core priority for my government. During our Security Council term, we served as a WPS shared commitment holder, and we remain committed to carrying that work forward. Next month, Seoul will host the eighth International Conference on Action with Women and Peace, a dedicated platform for women from diverse backgrounds to shape the conversation on peace processes. Together with partners such as UNFPA and the Women's Peace Humanitarian Fund, we are also supporting the recovery and the integration of survivors of gender-based violence and conflict-related sexual violence in Myanmar, while strengthening women's meaningful participation in peacebuilding in the Philippines. Our own experience of war has taught us that safeguarding children is both a moral imperative and an investment in lasting peace. Beyond ensuring accountability for grave violations, we must help children affected by conflict recover and rebuild their lives through psychosocial support, education, and community-based reintegration. The Republic of Korea contributes to these efforts through humanitarian assistance for education, water, sanitation, and hygiene, and basic health services, including through the Resilience for Children+ initiative launched with UNICEF in 2025. This year marks 20 years since the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Since becoming a state party in 2008, the Republic of Korea has continued to strengthen its legal and institutional frameworks to advance the full inclusion and participation of persons with disabilities. Last month, my government announced a comprehensive plan to establish state responsibility for the care of persons with developmental disabilities. supporting them across the life cycle and expanding opportunities for independent living in the community. We also take pride that Ms. Miyeon Kim, a Korean national, now chairs the CRPD Committee, and we remain committed to implementing its recommendations in good faith. UN emerging technologies. hold immense promise, yet they can be misused in ways that undermine human rights. Technology-facilitated violence disproportionately affects women and girls, and traffickers increasingly exploit digital platforms to recruit and control their victims. The Republic of Korea is confronting these risks both at home and with our partners. Domestically, we are tackling digital sex crimes by strengthening investigations, supporting victims, and promoting prevention through education. We also have put AI itself to work as a tool of protection, deploying AI-based systems to detect deepfake sexual imagery and swiftly remove it from online platforms. Internationally, we have recently launched a group of friends for combating technology-facilitated trafficking in persons with 28 member states to ensure that our collective response keeps pace with the evolving techniques of traffickers in the digital space. At the same time, new technologies can become powerful allies for human rights. We have long championed a human rights-based approach to new technologies, including by leading the relevant resolution in the Human Rights Council. The Republic of Korea envisions a global AI universal basic society in which no country and no person is left without access to the basic benefits of AI. and in which AI serves as a new engine to accelerate the realization of economic, social, and cultural rights. Turning to country situations, in his address to the General Assembly last month, President Lee Jae-myung presented three blueprints for inclusive, stable, and responsible peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula. On the basis of the universal value of human rights, the Republic of Korea remains committed to achieving tangible improvements in the human rights of the people in the DPRK, and will continue to cooperate closely with the international community toward this goal. Humanitarian cooperation that reaches the people of the DPRK can make a meaningful contribution in this regard. and we hope that opportunities will emerge to work together with the international community in areas such as public health, disaster response, and the climate crisis. We also seek the resolution of the long-standing humanitarian issues of the abductees, detainees, and on repatriated prisoners of war and separated families through inter-Korean dialogue and cooperation. On Myanmar, we urge all parties to cease violence and protect civilians. We hope that recent developments, such as the meeting between Aung San Suu Kyi and the international Committee of the Red Cross in August will lead to further efforts toward peace and reconciliation. We firmly support ASEAN's continued effort to implement the five-point consensus and will continue to provide humanitarian assistance to the people of Myanmar. Five years after the Taliban seized power, Afghan women and girls continue to bear the brunt of the deteriorating human rights situation. Girls remain barred from education beyond the sixth grade, and the recent decrees further weaken protection against child and post-marriage and gender-based violence. We once again call on the Taliban to reverse all discriminatory policies and to uphold Afghanistan's international human rights obligations. In Syria, Countless families are still searching for their loved ones, lost to decades of enforced disappearance and arbitrary detention. We believe transitional justice must be Syrian-led and victim-centred, and encourage close coordination between national commissions and the relevant international mechanisms. Madam Chair and distinguished colleagues, I begin today by speaking of the children behind the figures. It is for them and for everyone whose rights are denied that the work of this committee matters. Our resolutions will ultimately be judged not by the words we adopt here, but by the difference they make in people's lives. The Republic of Korea will continue to honor human rights at home and champion them abroad, working with all partners to turn our shared commitment into concrete change. I thank you.

I thank the permanent representative of the Republic of Korea. Dear colleagues, we have heard the last speaker in the general debate for this morning. The committee will reconvene this afternoon promptly at 3:00 p.m. to continue the general debate. The first three speakers will be reflected in the live list. The meeting is adjourned.
